name: David Fletcher - NHCB Certification: How to Build a New Homes Niche (Core Principles).txt
text:
NEW HOME CO-BROKER ACADEMY (NHCB)
Author & Founder: David R. Fletcher
Course: How to Build a New Homes Niche

CORE PHILOSOPHY & FOUNDATIONS:
1. The New Home Co-Broker Opportunity:
Real estate general agents frequently ignore new home construction because they assume on-site sales consultants are competitors or that builder commission policies are hostile. In truth, builders rely on general real estate agents (co-brokers) for 60% to 80% of their sales traffic. Agents who master the new homes niche unlock high-ticket inventory, reliable transactions, and clients who otherwise bypass traditional resale listings.

2. Understanding the On-Site Sales Consultant:
On-site sales agents represent the builder, not the buyer. However, they are not your adversaries—they are your greatest transaction partners. Their primary goal is maintaining sales pace (absorption rate) and selling out phases on schedule. Treat on-site agents with professional deference: call ahead before bringing clients, introduce yourself as a cooperating broker, and ask what inventory they are motivated to move.

3. The Mandatory Buyer Registration Rule:
Almost every builder enforces a strict client registration rule. The Golden Rule of New Home Co-Brokering is: You MUST accompany your client on their VERY FIRST VISIT to the model center or sales office. If the buyer walks in unrepresented and registers their name without you present, the builder's policy typically disallows co-broker commissions, even if you write the contract later. Many progressive builders now offer pre-registration online or by phone—always establish relationships with sales managers to verify their specific registration window (typically 30, 60, or 90 days).

4. Pricing Strategies: Concessions vs. Price Reductions:
Resale buyers expect price negotiation. In new construction, builders almost never reduce the base price of a home because base price cuts diminish appraisal values and comparable sales for the entire subdivision, jeopardizing existing loans in escrow. Instead, builders negotiate through builder incentives: closing cost credits, mortgage interest rate buydowns (e.g., 2-1 buydowns or permanent rate subsidies via affiliated lenders), design center upgrades, lot premium discounts, or included appliances.

5. Builder Contracts vs. Association Forms:
Builders utilize proprietary purchase agreements crafted by their legal counsel, not standard state board/association forms. Key differences include:
- Earnest money is often non-refundable after structural and design selection deadlines.
- Financing contingencies are closely tied to the builder's preferred lender.
- Completion dates are estimated target dates, with clauses allowing extensions for weather, permitting, and supply chain delays.
- Standard home inspection contingencies allow inspections, but the builder typically repairs items per their written warranty standards rather than renegotiating.

6. The VIP Preview Event Strategy:
One of David Fletcher's signature strategies for building a new home niche is hosting private VIP preview events in partnership with on-site sales consultants. Agents invite their SOI (Sphere of Influence), pre-approved buyers, and past clients to tour model homes before a public grand opening or phase release. The builder provides refreshments and early lot selection; the co-broker positions themselves as the expert insider who unlocks off-market opportunities.

name: David Fletcher - Overcoming Buyer Hesitations & Builder Negotiation Scripts.txt
text:
DAVID R. FLETCHER COACHING SCRIPTS & OBJECTION HANDLING

OBJECTION 1: "Why do I need a Realtor if the builder has sales agents on site?"
David's Guidance: The on-site sales counselor is an employee or exclusive agent of the builder. Their fiduciary duty is strictly to the builder's bottom line. Having an independent New Home Co-Broker gives the buyer objective representation at no additional cost to them (builder commissions are pre-budgeted marketing expenses that are not credited to the buyer if they come unrepresented). The co-broker helps compare builders, evaluate lot orientation and resale potential, review builder contracts, and monitor construction milestones.

OBJECTION 2: "We don't want to wait 6 to 9 months for construction."
David's Guidance: Emphasize 'Quick Move-In' (QMI) or 'Spec' homes. Builders start homes before securing buyers to keep framing crews and subcontractors working consistently. Spec homes are often 30 to 60 days from completion with finishes already selected, providing brand-new construction with resale-speed closings. Furthermore, quick move-ins near the end of a fiscal quarter or calendar year often carry the builder's most aggressive incentives.

OBJECTION 3: "Should I use the builder's preferred lender or my own bank?"
David's Guidance: Always advise the buyer to get pre-approved with an independent lender first to establish a baseline rate and closing costs. Then, review the builder's preferred lender package. Builders frequently offer thousands of dollars in closing cost concessions or below-market interest rate buydowns only available through their affiliated lender. While the buyer has the statutory legal right to choose their lender, the financial incentives offered by builder-affiliated lenders often make them the most cost-effective choice.

OBJECTION 4: "Can we negotiate the price down?"
David's Guidance: Never tell a buyer you cannot negotiate. Instead, guide them on WHERE to negotiate. Explain that asking for a $20,000 price drop will almost certainly be rejected, but asking for a $20,000 credit toward an interest rate buydown or design center credit is frequently accepted. Educate the buyer that a 1% rate buydown lowers monthly payments far more than a modest price cut.
